This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder. The U.S. and Israel are preparing plans for a possible attack on Iran in early November after the U.S. midterm elections.
That's according to a person briefed on the matter speaking to NPR from Tel Aviv. NPR's Daniel Estrin has more.
The person briefed on the U.S. and Israel's war planning spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity to discuss the preparations.
The person said Israel had initially planned to strike Iran in mid-October about two weeks before Israeli elections October 27th, but President Trump objected.
The person briefed said the U.S. is now amassing forces in the region to be ready for an attack by early November after U.S. midterms November 3rd,
but that these preparations could also be part of a campaign to pressure Iran to reach a diplomatic deal.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is campaigning for reelection on a threat to topple Iran's regime.
Daniel Estrin, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
President Trump is back in Washington after wrapping up his latest midterm campaign rally.
He arrived late Wednesday night from South Carolina, where he campaigned for Darlene Graham's U.S. Senate campaign.
He is to hold another rally in Iowa Thursday.
During a campaign stop in Ohio on Wednesday, Vice President J.D. Vance downplayed an attack ad from Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for governor.
The controversial ad features the estranged mother of Ramaswamy's opponent, Democratic candidate Amy Acton, who was removed from her mother's custody when she was 12 years old after her stepfather was charged with sexually assaulting her.
Vance was asked about the ad during a stop in Cincinnati.
Whether the ad was appropriate or not is not really my concern.
What is my concern is who's going to govern the next generation of American government.
Acton calls the Ramaswamy ad despicable. She says she has not spoken to her mother in some 50 years.
New Mexico judge has ordered Meta to pay $25 billion for deceiving users about privacy.
NPR's Bobby Allen reports on what the state says is one of the largest ever verdicts against a tech giant.
A jury found Meta was responsible for violating New Mexico consumer protection laws after misleading users about its handling of a third party app connected to the 2018 Cambridge Analytica data breach when a consulting firm data mined tens of millions of Facebook users without their consent.
New Mexico sued the tech giant, saying the company had misrepresented just how safe users' data was on its social media platforms.
State authorities argued that Meta was liable for tens of millions of violations of the law, and each penalty carried a fine of $5,000,
which is how the judge in the case ordered Meta to pay New Mexico $25 billion.
Meta did not return a request for comment, but has vowed to appeal.
The case harkens back to an era when tech controversies were dominated by fights over data harvesting, not AI.
Bobby Allen, NPR News.
This is NPR.
The French government has promised massive security forces on the streets for a demonstration called for this Saturday.
Six months ahead of France's presidential election, the French far right, capitalizing, almost described as the seeming failure of President Macron's government to keep order.
And Biers-Eleanor Beardsley reports from Paris.
Speaking in a radio interview on "Françon Faux," far right candidate Marine Le Pen said the government has lost control of everything.
"It's chaos. Immigration chaos, security chaos, and budgetary chaos," said Le Pen.
"We must get this situation under control."
After being beaten twice by President Macron, Paul Sholopin is the front runner in next spring's presidential election.
Macron is not allowed to seek a third term.
What started as a student movement for better facilities and more teachers has turned into a general protest movement against the high cost of living and inequalities.
President Macron, who's been in office 10 years, is being blamed by the far right and far left for everything.
Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News, Paris.
NFL commissioner Roger Goodell says he is comfortable with security ahead of Sunday's NFL game in Paris.
Goodell said Wednesday that he has spoken with Secretary of State Marco Rubio and that officials are in touch with authorities in France.
The threat of severe weather ongoing in parts of the southwest, the National Weather Service warning of the potential for flash flooding from excessive rainfall in northern and central Arizona through late Thursday evening.
Storms Wednesday brought golf ball-sized hail and strong winds that toppled trees in Flagstaff and Mesa.
I'm Jyle Snyder. This is NPR News.

Vance downplays Ramaswamy attack ad featuring Amy Acton's estranged mother in Cincinnati

French government plans heavy security for Saturday protest as Marine Le Pen attacks Macron
NFL's Roger Goodell says he is comfortable with security for Sunday's Paris game
Storms bring golf ball-sized hail and flash flood warnings to Arizona
